claims.explanation: Crizotinib selectively kills cancer lines that depend on oncogenic ALK or ROS1 kinase signaling, most commonly through EML4-ALK or other ALK/ROS1 gene fusions, and to a lesser extent through MET amplification or exon 14 skipping. The drug's annotated targets (ALK, MET) and clinical literature show that fusion-positive lung cancers are exquisitely sensitive, while lines lacking these alterations are largely unaffected. The virtual-cell similarity to the ALK inhibitor NVP-TAE684 further supports ALK pathway inhibition as the primary selective mechanism.

features.basis: ALK gene rearrangement/fusion creates an oncogenic driver that is directly inhibited by crizotinib (clinical trials in ALK-positive NSCLC)
ROS1 rearrangement defines a molecular subset of NSCLC with high response rates to crizotinib
MET is a direct crizotinib target; MET amplification or exon 14 skipping can drive oncogenic dependence
High ALK expression from fusion alleles correlates with pathway addiction and crizotinib sensitivity
ROS1 fusion-driven expression marks tumors responsive to crizotinib
MET overexpression/amplification can increase dependence on MET signaling inhibited by crizotinib
EML4-ALK fusion is the most common ALK rearrangement sensitizing NSCLC to crizotinib
EGFR-mutant lung cancers are typically ALK/ROS1 fusion-negative and respond poorly to crizotinib monotherapy
KRAS mutations are mutually exclusive with ALK/ROS1 fusions and predict lack of crizotinib sensitivity
TP53 mutations may reduce dependence on ALK/ROS1 signaling and associate with poorer response to targeted therapy
NF1 loss activates RAS/MAPK independent of ALK, potentially bypassing crizotinib inhibition
PIK3CA mutations can activate PI3K/AKT downstream of ALK, reducing sensitivity to ALK inhibition
